notes.meaning: King Abijah died and was buried with his royal ancestors in Jerusalem, and his son Asa took the throne. The Lord gave Judah ten years of peace, partly because the northern kingdom was still weak from an earlier defeat. Asa used this quiet decade to set his kingdom in order.

Asa chose to live and rule in a way that pleased God. He did not simply do what was popular or right in his own eyes, but obeyed God's law. He became the first king of Judah after the kingdom split to lead widespread spiritual reform.

Asa cleared out the foreign altars, idol pillars, and carved wooden poles that had stood since the time of Solomon. These false gods had pulled the people away from the Lord. By smashing them, Asa took an active stand against idolatry.

The king ordered the people of Judah to turn back to the God of their ancestors. He issued a royal command telling them to follow God's law and live by His rules. Asa used his authority to guide the nation into faithful worship.

Asa extended his work beyond the capital, removing idol shrines and sun altars from every city in Judah. Because the king honored God by removing these false places of worship, the land stayed peaceful and calm under his rule.

During this peaceful season, Asa built strong walls and defenses around key cities in Judah. No foreign enemy attacked him during these years because the Lord gave him rest. He understood that true rest comes as a gift from God.

Asa urged his leaders to build up their towns with walls, towers, gates, and heavy bars while they still had peace. He told them that God had given them rest on every side because they sought Him. The people followed his lead, worked hard, and prospered.

Asa assembled a large army of 580,000 brave soldiers. The men of Judah carried heavy body shields and spears for fighting up close, while the men of Benjamin were skilled archers who carried smaller shields. Together they formed a well-trained defense force.

A leader named Zerah the Cushite marched against Judah with an enormous army of one million soldiers and three hundred chariots. This invading force advanced deep into Judah's border, reaching the town of Mareshah. Asa's army was now heavily outnumbered.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historians suggest Zerah may have been a Nubian general serving the Egyptian pharaoh Osorkon I, though his name has not yet been discovered in surviving ancient Egyptian records.

notes.meaning: Asa did not wait behind city walls for the enemy to surround him, but marched out to the frontier. He arranged his army in battle formation in the valley of Zephathah near Mareshah. Setting his troops in the valley gave his smaller force a better position for the fight.

Before the battle started, Asa cried out to the Lord in prayer. He admitted his army was weak compared to this massive host, but declared that numbers mean nothing to God. Asa asked the Lord to help them and protect His own honor against mortal men.

The Lord answered Asa's prayer by striking the enemy army with sudden terror and confusion. The Cushite soldiers broke ranks and ran for their lives before Asa and his men. God gave Judah the victory before the fighting even got fully underway.

Asa and his soldiers chased the enemy more than twenty miles south toward the Philistine city of Gerar. The Cushites were crushed so thoroughly that they could not regroup or fight back. Judah then collected a massive amount of valuable goods left behind on the battlefield.

Asa's army also struck the towns around Gerar that had allied with the invading force. The Lord placed a deep dread upon these cities, so the inhabitants could not resist. Judah captured a great amount of supplies and treasure from them.

Judah's troops also overran the desert camps belonging to nomadic herdsmen who had supported the invading army. They captured large herds of sheep and camels to bring home. The soldiers then returned to Jerusalem, celebrating the deliverance God had given them.
